sets.tower: Starbase launch tower at dusk. far: SpaceBackdrop #0A0A1E with a thin orange horizon band and first stars; mid: a tall dark lattice tower in pale rim light with two big steel 'chopstick' arms reaching out to the right; a silver-black Starship stack beside it; near: GroundPlane of dark concrete with pale rim and floodlights with bloom. setp.arms 0..1 = chopstick arms open (0) to closed (1); setp.ship 0..1 = ship height (0 on the pad, 1 gone; also 0.5 = hovering at catch height between the arms); setp.fire 0..1 = engine flame size; setp.tint 'dusk' (default) | 'night'.
sets.ascent: Side view of the rocket climbing. A tall silver-black Starship stack with a long orange flame rises through a darkening blue sky into black, tiny Gulf of Mexico coastline below. setp.t 0..1 = altitude (0 near ground, 1 in space); setp.stage 0|1 = 0 stacked, 1 booster separated and tumbling back.
sets.booster: Super Heavy booster returning. A big silver booster with grid fins falls over a dark sea, flame at the base; setp.t 0..1 = descent; setp.abort 0..1 = a red ABORT flash appears and the booster swerves out over the water, ending in a splash and orange fireball at 1.
sets.orbit: Earth from low orbit. A huge curved Earth limb (deep blue, pale rim, cyan atmosphere band, tiny city-light dots on the dark side), stars above, a silver-black Starship small in the middle with a faint trail. setp.t 0..1 = ship position along the limb; setp.lights 0..1 = night-side city lights.
sets.deploy: Close view of the ship's open payload door with flat Starlink satellites popping out one by one like a Pez dispenser, drifting away over Earth's blue limb. setp.n 0..26 = how many satellites have left (each a small flat dark panel with a gold solar-array glint).
sets.loop: Orbit diagram, top-down on Earth. Earth disc at centre (blue-green, pale rim), a thin cream circular orbit ring at 260 km, a small ship dot moving around it, small tick marks for each completed lap. setp.laps 0..14 = laps completed (ship position and ticks), setp.glow 0|1 = gold ring glow.
sets.reentry: Ship falling into the atmosphere, belly first. Dark upper sky fading to deep blue at the bottom; the silver-black ship tilted horizontally with its tile-covered belly down; a hot plasma sheath around the leading edges with orange, pink and white layers and sparks streaming upward. setp.heat 0..1 = plasma intensity and sparks; setp.alt 0..1 = height (1 high, 0 near ground).
sets.hover: Ship returning to the tower, near. The tall ship falls tail-first with a flame beneath it between the two open chopstick arms of the tower, dusk sky, dust blowing at the base. setp.t 0..1 = descent (0 high above, 1 hovering at the arms); setp.arms 0..1 = arms closing (1 = closed around the ship); setp.dust 0..1 = swirling dust.
sets.ops: SpaceX launch control room. far: wall of dark screens with glowing cream trajectory curves; mid: rows of desks, headset lamps, no faces; near: carpet GroundPlane with pale rim. setp.tension 0..1 = number of screens flashing amber; setp.ok 1 turns all screens green with a soft pulse.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.ship: Small Starship icon: tall silver-black cylinder with a pointed nose, two small flaps at top and two at the bottom, 4 px dark outline, soft rim light; pp.flame true adds an orange flame at the base; pp.s scale.
props.booster: Small Super Heavy booster icon: a wide silver cylinder with grid fins at the top and a ring of tiny engines at the base; pp.flame true adds a flame.
props.starlink: Small flat Starlink satellite icon: dark rectangular panel with a pale outline and a gold solar-array glint; pp.s scale.
props.tile: Single black heat-shield tile, square with rounded corners, 4 px outline, pale rim, a tiny pencil signature on it; pp.glow true adds a warm orange glow.
props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.stopwatch: Round outlined stopwatch, cream face, red button on top; pp.from..pp.to seconds: hand sweeps and digits count.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.sign: Hand-painted sign on a post, cream board, dark outline, pp.text in FONTS.hand (max 12 chars).

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back (headTilt up), arms hang loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms raised over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation (yaw/spin) across the shot while looking up.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point at the sky at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

film.vo: Twenty-two hours ago, you left this tower.
Now you are falling back at it.
Plasma on every edge.
And two steel arms are waiting.
No landing legs. No parachute. Just a catch.
SpaceX did it on Saturday the fourteenth.
So what if you rode it all the way?
What if you rode Starship around Earth fourteen times?
Here are the rules.
You ride Ship forty-two, the top half of Starship.
Its partner, Booster twenty-two, does the heavy lifting.
Together they are forty-one stories tall.
You will be on board for twenty-two and a half hours.
The catch at the end has never been tried on a ship.
Buckle up. Friday, thirteenth of November.
Four forty-seven in the afternoon, Texas time.
Twelve million pounds of fuel sit under your feet.
Liquid oxygen. Liquid methane.
Thirty-three engines wake up beneath you.
And you rise.
A forty-one-story megarocket, climbing.
Faster. Higher. The sky goes dark.
Minutes in, the stack comes apart.
One of the booster's engines may have dropped out.
You keep climbing. Six engines. All good.
Below you, the booster turns for home.
It plans to land in the same arms you will.
SpaceX has caught a booster three times before.
This time, an alarm goes off.
Low fuel mass. The burn ended early.
The booster checks its own position.
It is not where it should be.
So it aborts itself. Out over the Gulf.
One half of the dream goes into the water.
Now it is all on you.
Twenty-six minutes after liftoff, one engine relights.
For twenty seconds.
And the engine goes quiet. You are in orbit.
Only the second time Starship has ever done this.
Two hundred seventy-five kilometres up.
You are carrying twenty-six passengers.
Starlink satellites, stacked like a pez dispenser.
Pop. Pop. Pop.
Twelve gone in the first hour.
One of them turns its camera back at you.
It is checking your heat shield, tile by tile.
One tile was installed by MrBeast.
No pressure, tile.
At the one hour seventeen mark, the last one leaves.
But your day is not over. You still have to get down.
Now you coast. And coast.
Twenty-six thousand kilometres an hour.
About ninety-six minutes to circle the planet.
Lap three. Lap four. Southeast Asia, then the Indian Ocean.
You see a sunrise on every single lap.
Seven hours in, mission control gets a choice.
Bring you down early, in the ocean off Chile?
Or let you stay?
Go. You stay in space.
Lap ten. Lap eleven. Longest Starship flight ever.
Heat shield data comes back clean. The heat shield is fine.
Hour twenty. The last go or no-go.
Every team polls go. Even the tower.
Three twenty-three in the afternoon. The deorbit burn.
Ten seconds. One engine.
That is all it takes to fall out of the sky.
The air starts to bite.
Your leading edges glow.
Orange. Then pink. Then white.
Heat-shield tiles stand between you and the fire.
You cannot see out. You cannot steer.
The ship does it for you. Flaps, flipping, falling.
Then the plasma fades.
Texas is below you. And so is the tower.
Now the hard part. You have to land on your tail.
The engines relight. The ship flips upright.
Dust rolls out from the pad like a storm.
The arms open wide.
You are falling toward two steel rails.
The engine slows you almost to a stop.
A hover. Right between the arms.
The arms close.
Engines off.
Four-twenty in the afternoon, eastern time.
Twenty-two and a half hours after you left.
You flew around Earth fourteen times.
And you are standing exactly where you started.
The commentator called it the holy grail of spaceflight.
Plummeting through fire, snatched out of the air by steel.
The booster was caught three times. The ship, never. Until today.
The ship flies higher and comes in faster.
That is why it was the tougher target.
A rocket you can catch is a rocket you can reuse.
And reuse makes spaceflight cheaper.
NASA is counting on it for its Artemis astronauts.
Starship will practise docking with Orion next year.
So the next time you look up, remember.
Something huge can fall from the sky and be caught like a cup.
Which part scared you most: the launch, the plasma, or the catch?
Tomorrow: another what if, another piece of the sky.

short.vo: You just fell out of orbit.
Twenty-two and a half hours ago, you left this tower.
Thirty-three engines. Twelve million pounds of fuel.
The booster aborts. You keep going.
Then twenty-six satellites pop out of your belly.
Fourteen laps. Twenty-six thousand kilometres an hour.
One tile on your belly was put there by MrBeast.
Ten-second burn. Then plasma on every edge.
You hover. Right between the arms.
The arms close. You are caught.
A ship has never been caught before. Until Saturday.
Full film on the channel. Tomorrow: another what if.
